title: Goodnight Stories | A Withering Aria
subtitle: A dead aria, a synesthetic dream, a drink waiting for you to wake.
body:
## I. Absinthe

I cannot remember names, people’s faces, or what cars look like.

The doctor said it was a kind of neurological trauma, arising from sensory overcompensation after hearing loss. Like staring too intently at a line of text for too long, until the characters twist into shapes you no longer recognize.

But I had not truly lost my hearing. I simply could no longer distinguish pitch. First my absolute pitch fell into disorder; later, even relative pitch became blurred. Crowds, engines, rhythms, shouts—all were like iron objects soaked in warm water, carrying echoes with no discernible source.

I moved from the city to the sea, without goodbye or explanation.

There is always a place on a cruise ship, especially for a musician willing to play for tourists drinking cocktails.

I became the ship’s bar pianist. Every evening from seven to ten, I played jazz. Not particularly well; I could not tell whether the notes went astray. In any case, once everyone was drunk, they could not tell either.

My playing was like the sea: floating, neither deep nor shallow, with no need to arrive anywhere.

## II. Kirschwasser

Until that night, when she ordered a cocktail with a strange name, like a spell with a Latin ending.

**Aria Morta**. Its color was like red ink dried on old writing paper.

The waiter brought it to me. I only glanced at it and did not touch it.

I never drank. Someone who practices an instrument will not allow alcohol to damage the nerves. Even if I only played piano now, my fingers and ears were still vessels of memory, allowing not a drop of wavering.

But that night, I did not refuse. I did not drink it, yet I kept it. It stood quietly beside the piano, as though a portion of sin and desire had been placed beside God’s pillow.

She had not signed her name, only left a note: “It’s rare to find someone who can hide the flavor of Goldberg in jazz.”

I began searching for her among the audience. But I could not recognize her. Each day’s faces were alike; smiles beneath the lights were like the moon on water, shattering at a tremor. Perhaps she had come countless times. Perhaps she had never come at all.

## III. Crème de Violette

From that day, my room changed too.

Sometimes the ceiling was wet, as though an unrecorded rain had just fallen. Droplets quietly seeped from the corners, one by one, striking the air as though keeping time for a dream. I tilted my head back, parted my lips slightly, and caught them: damp, but not salty, tasting like some long-forgotten dew.

Sometimes vines grew wildly from the walls, their leaves carrying a faintly warm green glow, winding around the mirror. I reached out to grasp them, but the vines coiled around me instead, turning me until even my reflection was swallowed with me, dissolved into a softly whispering green.

Another night, the window suddenly opened by itself. Swarms of blue butterflies poured in on the sea breeze, circled the room several times, then flew away without a sound. Only two remained, settling on my outstretched fingers. Their wings moved slowly, like the breath of a lover whispering by one’s ear, unwilling to disturb.

I was not afraid. I knew it was music returning to find me in another way. I began to see music. It was the opening of some kind of synesthesia—perhaps compensation, perhaps a curse. I no longer needed to listen; I learned to feel with my eyes, my palms, and my lips.

## IV. Blackcurrant Bitters

The night before we docked, I went onto the bar’s stage.

This time I did not play jazz. I had not written the pieces, nor had they been written for piano. They did not originally belong to my fingers, yet that night they flowed from my keys.

**Barber – Violin Concerto, Op.14**

The notes were like water, falling drop by drop into the cracks in the wooden floor late at night. The melody was gentle, like a damp dream slowly rising to the surface. Every note was like a drop of dew seeping from the ceiling, striking the air with an unspoken goodbye. I saw the first time she entered the bar: like those droplets that night, quietly and soundlessly seeping into the softest layer of my heart.

**Sibelius – Violin Concerto in D minor**

The opening melody was like a vine winding upward, growing slowly and calmly. The notes circled in the air, as though something were being quietly drawn up and tightened. I played very slowly, as though I too had been wound inside. My reflection on the piano was swallowed little by little by the green melody. The vines entwined my fingertips and the shadow of my past. This was what I had never dared admit: how deeply I wished dream and reality could exchange places, so I would not have to wake.

**The Butterfly Lovers' Violin Concerto**

I did not play it in its original order. I began with “Transformation into Butterflies,” those high notes everyone says sound like farewell, like butterflies passing over the human world one last time. But I brought them forward, as though revealing fate early only to keep it from falling at the end. Then came “Resistance to Marriage.” The notes trembled like a gap desperately tearing open between two worlds. I let them pause there for a moment, just as I had once refused every plea to stay and chosen to drift at sea. Finally, I played “Meeting.” That gentlest melody, with no cries and no flight: only two people looking up for the first time, lingering in each other’s eyes for one extra second. I stretched that second across three full measures, as though winning myself a belated first encounter. When I reached this point, I closed my eyes and felt a kind of light pass through the stage.

## V. Bergamot Eau de Cologne

When I opened my eyes, she was walking toward me from the far end of the crowd. She wore a moonlight-gray dress, its hem lifted lightly by the air like a butterfly just taking flight. Gently, she handed me a glass of **Aria Morta**. “Come to my performance.”

I lifted the glass and drank it in one swallow. In that moment, the alcohol did not burn me. Only a faintly cool residual warmth sank down my throat.

I said nothing, only held out an instrument case. She took it and opened it, showing no surprise, but I saw her eyelashes tremble slightly. It was a Stradivarius violin.

“Your Guarneri has brought me countless dreams,” I said softly. “But I believe someone who can hear the trace of the Goldberg Variations unconsciously woven into my playing will be this violin’s best new companion.”

She did not answer, only held the case tightly, as though catching something that had fallen from me.

Who says a second-rate pianist cannot once have been a genius violinist?

## VI. Butterfly Pea Petals

On the day the ship docked, I did not see her off, nor say goodbye.

I sat alone in the empty bar and played the final part of the Goldberg Variations: **Aria da capo**.

All the variations had passed; back to the first melody. No tears, and no regrets.

I closed my eyes and saw her in the spaces between the notes. That night, wearing her moonlight-gray dress, she walked toward me from the far end of the light.

From my lips, a name emerged softly:

“Hahn.”

So I could remember, after all.

## 🎁 Appendix: The “Aria Morta” Recipe (Hidden Easter Egg)

It is said that after the pianist died, someone found a sheet of paper dampened by seawater in a drawer of the ship’s old bar. It recorded a strange name and its recipe. Later, this drink began appearing in bars that opened for only one hour at night. It was never on the menu; only those who understood knew to order it.

“Whoever drinks it must be prepared to remember a melody they once forgot with their own hands.”

**Ingredients:**

- 15 ml absinthe
- 30 ml kirschwasser
- 10 ml crème de violette
- 1 drop blackcurrant bitters
- Bergamot eau de cologne
- Garnish: butterfly pea petals (symbolizing “echo”)

**Method:**

1. Add ice to a mixing glass, pour in all the spirits, and stir slowly for 20 seconds.
2. Strain into a small old-fashioned glass (Nick & Nora cup).
3. Lightly spray with bergamot eau de cologne.
4. Leave it for 5 seconds—let the first melody disappear into the air.

**How to Drink:**

Lift it in silence, murmur its name, “Aria Morta,” then close your eyes and drink.

When you open them again, perhaps you will hear the song you yourself forgot.

*Translator’s note: The appendix is a fictional recipe within the story. Eau de cologne is perfume, not an edible cocktail ingredient.*
